reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and Design Methods
chapter_title: Techniques for Maintaining Stable Drilled Shaft Excavations

sections.title: Naturally Stable Conditions
sections.body: Stable excavation conditions exist in dry soil, strong cohesive or cemented soils, and intact rock. Stability depends on hole diameter and depth, surface loads, construction vibrations, and time hole must remain open. Local experience provides guidance but does not eliminate need for site-specific information. Mixed conditions are common — cohesive overburden may allow dry open-hole drilling while underlying sands require additional support. Water-bearing sand below clay overburden can cause flowing sands or bottom heave if groundwater level exceeds base of excavation. Rock with low permeability (shale, chalk, massive rock) may permit dry excavation even below groundwater. Add water to hole during excavation of permeable rock (porous limestone, sandstone) rather than allowing inflow that brings fines or causes sloughing.
key_points: Naturally stable: dry soil, strong cohesive/cemented soils, intact rock
Mixed conditions common — separate methods may be used for different strata
Cohesive soils into water-bearing sand: risk of flowing sands or bottom heave
Add water to permeable rock holes rather than allowing inflow with fines

sections.title: Temporary Casing
sections.body: [p. 5-3] Temporary casing is used to stabilize the drilled shaft excavation and then removed after or during placement of fluid concrete; contractors emphasize that it is essentially a tool, so it is sometimes termed temporary tool casing. It remains in place until the fluid concrete has been placed to a level sufficient to withstand surrounding ground and groundwater pressures, and is then removed; additional concrete may be placed as the casing is pulled to maintain the pressure balance, the fluid pressure of the concrete being relied upon for borehole stability (see also Chapter 3). When approved by the engineer, temporary casing used solely to support the excavation may be left in place, and the engineer must then assess its influence on the axial and lateral resistance of the completed shaft. In some soils, such as soft cohesive soils prone to squeezing or bulging if the casing is removed, the engineer may require the temporary casing to remain permanently through potentially unstable layers. Temporary casing must be cleaned thoroughly after each use to have low shearing resistance to the movement of fluid concrete: casing with a rough interior may drag on the concrete column as it is lifted, cause necking or voids, displace the reinforcement or even become stuck. The casing should be free of soil, lubricants and other deleterious material. Subsections: 5.2.1 Types and Dimensions; 5.2.2 Installation and Extraction; 5.2.3 Possible Effects on Axial and Lateral Resistance; 5.2.4 Removing Casing after Concrete Sets.
key_points: Temporary (tool) casing is removed during or after concrete placement, once the concrete head balances ground and water pressures
Left in place only with the engineer's approval, who then assesses its effect on axial and lateral resistance
The engineer may require it to stay through soft cohesive soils prone to squeezing or bulging
Clean after each use: a rough interior drags on the concrete, causing necking, voids, cage displacement or stuck casing
sections.applicability: Caving soils, below-water-table conditions, mixed soil/rock profiles

sections.title: Types and Dimensions
sections.body: [pp. 5-3 to 5-5] Most drilling contractors keep a large supply of temporary casing of various diameters and lengths (Figure 5-3); stockpiled casing may be welded or cut to suit a project. Where the excavation is to be advanced below the casing in the dry, the casing must sometimes be seated into an impervious formation such as rock, normally using the casing as a tool with twisting or driving forces; its end may have cutting teeth or extra thickness to aid installation and avoid distortion. ADSC (The International Association of Foundation Drilling) has adopted the outside diameter as a standard, in traditional units (e.g., 36-in. O.D.), because used pipe in O.D. sizes costs much less than specially rolled pipe with a specified I.D. (ADSC, 1995); special sizes cost more and need fabrication lead time. O.D. sizes are ordinarily available in 6-inch increments from 18 to 120 inches; larger sizes (Figure 5-4) typically need special order. Manufactured segmental casing typically comes in metric sizes, so the design should allow some flexibility on sizes where temporary casing is anticipated: e.g., 1.2 m (47.25 in.) for a 48-in. size, or 3 m (118 in.) for a 10-ft (120-in.) size, can normally be accommodated; otherwise the contractor would be forced to upsize at considerable cost to use segmental casing. If the casing size is not specified, most contractors use a casing with an O.D. 6 inches larger than the specified shaft diameter below the casing, to pass a drilling tool of the specified diameter; where boulders are anticipated or telescoping casing is used, the first casing may be more than 6 inches larger. The contractor is usually responsible for casing strength against soil, rock and internal and external fluid pressures. Most steel casing has a wall thickness of at least 0.325 inches, casings larger than 48 inch O.D. tend to be thicker, and installation by vibratory or impact hammer may need a greater thickness than casing placed in an oversized hole; most contractors select wall thickness by experience, but if workers must enter an excavation the casing should be designed with an appropriate factor of safety against collapse. The allowable lateral pressure on a casing is a complex problem beyond the scope of the manual, generally one of preventing buckling under external soil and water pressure; factors include diameter, wall thickness, out-of-roundness, corrosion, minor defects, combined stresses, microseismic events, instability of soil on slopes and other sources of nonuniform pressure, and pressure increasing with depth. Semi-rigid liners (corrugated sheet metal, plain sheet metal, pressed fiber, plastic or other tubes) can be used for liners or surface casing left in place, most often to restrain unstable surface soil or to aid the shaft to column connection, e.g., corrugated sheet metal where the concrete cutoff is below working grade; rigid liners such as precast concrete pipe are occasionally used. Rotators and/or oscillators with segmental casing (Figure 5-5) are increasingly used for large diameter, deep shafts: the casing is advanced ahead of the excavation, supporting it without slurry for sidewall stability, although slurry or water may still be needed to prevent base heave; soil inside is removed with clam, hammer-grab or rotary tools. The casing is typically high strength steel, often double-wall, with flush joints that transmit torque (either direction), compression and tension between segments. Casing joints can instead be welded to standard pipe (Figure 5-6), in which case the joint protrudes into the casing.
key_points: Contractors stock casing; stockpiled casing is welded or cut to suit
ADSC standard: O.D. sizes in 6-inch increments from 18 to 120 inches (ADSC, 1995); larger sizes by special order
Segmental casing is metric: allow e.g. 1.2 m (47.25 in.) for 48 in. or 3 m (118 in.) for 10 ft
Unspecified casing size: typically O.D. 6 inches larger than the shaft below; more with boulders or telescoping
Wall thickness usually at least 0.325 in.; thicker above 48 in. O.D. or for hammer installation
Design casing against collapse with a factor of safety if workers enter the hole
Semi-rigid liners (corrugated or sheet metal, pressed fiber, plastic) for surface casing left in place
Segmental casing with oscillators/rotators supports deep large holes without slurry; joints transmit torque, compression and tension

sections.title: Installation and Extraction of Temporary Casing
sections.body: [pp. 5-6 to 5-7] Temporary casing is sometimes placed into an oversized drilled hole and seated into the underlying formation (5.2.2.1), but it can also be advanced ahead of or together with the excavation (5.2.2.2). Each method may have implications for design because of its effect on side resistance in the zone through which the casing is installed (5.2.3).
key_points: Casing seated through a drilled hole, or advanced ahead of the excavation
The method can affect side resistance in the cased zone
sections.applicability: Choosing a temporary casing installation method and its design implications

sections.title: Casing Seated Through Drilled Hole
sections.body: [pp. 5-7 to 5-9] Temporary casing can be placed through a pre-drilled hole to seat it into an underlying, more stable formation. The hole may be made by the wet method with slurry, or without fluid if the soil stands briefly and seepage is small, often the case when drilling quickly through residual soil to rock, the casing then preventing cave-ins during the slower rock excavation; water-bearing sands near the surface may need the starter hole drilled with slurry, and some contractors use polymer slurry just to lubricate the casing for removal. The excavation below may proceed dry if the casing is seated with a watertight seal into relatively impermeable clay, chalk or rock; a twister bar on the kelly lets the rig apply torque and crowd to the casing (J-slots in the casing top, Figure 5-7), and the casing end usually has cutting teeth suited to the material (Figure 5-8). A good seal can be very difficult where the rock surface is steeply sloping or highly irregular, or where seams or joints let water in below the casing, so the casing often must go some distance into rock and the design should allow flexibility in the casing tip elevation; an irregular hard surface risks deflecting the casing off alignment, breaking teeth or bending the casing under excessive downforce. Telescoping casing (Figure 5-9) uses more than one piece: a larger hole and casing at the surface, then a smaller hole and casing below, possibly through several steps, with the I.D. (O.D. if excavation does not proceed below the casing) of the lowest casing at least the specified shaft diameter. Smaller cranes and ancillary equipment suffice. The O.D. of a lower section is typically at least 6 inches smaller than that of the section above, although larger differences may be used. The procedure is most often used for shafts bearing on or socketed into rock where no skin friction is counted in the cased soil or rock; the contractor must take care that removing the smaller casings does not disturb the larger ones or deposit water, slurry or debris behind casings still in place, contaminating the concrete. Telescoping casing may also case through boulder fields, boulders removed as the casing is screwed ahead to refusal and a smaller casing advanced through the first. Concrete placement in a telescoped hole is in Chapter 7.
key_points: Pre-drilled hole made wet (slurry) or dry if it stands and seepage is small; polymer may lubricate the casing
A watertight seat in clay, chalk or rock allows a dry excavation below; twister bar, J-slots and cutting teeth
Sloping or irregular rock or open joints make sealing hard: allow flexibility in casing tip elevation
Telescoping casing: each lower casing typically at least 6 inches smaller in O.D.; lowest I.D. at least the shaft diameter
Used mostly for rock-bearing shafts with no skin friction counted in the cased zone
Removing inner casings must not disturb outer casings or trap water, slurry or debris behind them

sections.title: Casing Advanced Ahead of Excavation
sections.body: [p. 5-9] The contractor may advance casing ahead of the excavation where the hole will not stand open for short periods or where slurry drilling is less attractive in cost or performance. There are two primary methods: driving with a vibratory hammer (5.2.2.2.1), or twisting with the drill rig or oscillator/rotator equipment (5.2.2.2.2). In either case soil friction on the casing wall must be reduced enough for the casing to advance: the vibratory hammer temporarily reduces the strength of the soil along the wall, and twisting relies on a small overcut by the casing shoe or cutting teeth. These techniques let the soil arch around the circular excavation, the radial horizontal stresses on the casing being transferred into hoop stresses around the hole (Figure 5-10).
key_points: Used where the hole will not stand or slurry is less attractive
Vibratory driving, or twisting by drill rig or oscillator/rotator
Side friction is reduced by vibration or by an overcut, letting the soil arch (radial stress to hoop stress)
figures: Figure 5-10: Reduced horizontal stress due to soil arching, which develops as soil moves inward
sections.applicability: Advancing temporary casing ahead of the excavation in unstable soils

sections.title: Vibro-Driven Casing
sections.body: [pp. 5-10 to 5-11] When casing is driven, a vibratory hammer is almost always used for temporary casing; an impact hammer may install permanent casing, but temporary casing needs a vibratory hammer for extraction, since impact-driven casing may be impossible to remove due to increased friction. Jetting could aid installation in principle, but not extraction, since jet water could harm the fluid concrete. Vibratory installation can cause significant vibrations that affect nearby structures, or settlement in loose sands affecting structures and utilities; attenuation depends on hammer and casing size, operating frequency, soil and rock properties, local stratigraphy, groundwater and other site-specific factors. In most cases vibrations are extremely small at 50 to 70 ft from the source, but may extend farther when penetrating hard or cemented layers. Where sensitive structures are nearby, vibration monitoring should be in the installation plan; it helps avoid damage, documents against claims, and measurements during technique and test shaft installations at various radial distances are valuable before moving into congested production locations (reference: Construction Vibrations, Dowding, 2000). Vibratory installation is most effective in sandy soils and to penetrate through sands into a clay or marl below. The hammer clamps to the casing top (Figure 5-11), often reinforced with extra thickness; the vibration often temporarily liquefies a thin zone of soil at the casing wall so that the casing penetrates under the weight of casing plus hammer, particularly effective in sandy soils with shallow groundwater. Penetrating an underlying hard layer such as cemented sand or rock may be difficult or impossible, and twisting the casing with the rig to seat it in rock is likely ineffective because of soil side resistance once vibration stops. Generally the whole casing length is vibrated in before excavating inside; in particularly dense soils it can be installed by alternately driving and drilling out the plug, typically in sections joined by welding. In relief drilling, an auger breaks up a hard layer below the casing so the casing can follow; if the soil would not stand, the auger rotation can be reversed on extraction to leave the soil in place. The casing must be removed while the concrete is still fluid: the powered hammer typically first drives the casing down a few inches under the weight of casing and hammer to break it free, and the crane then pulls it up, leaving the concrete-filled hole (Figure 5-11 shows the start of removal).
key_points: Vibratory hammer for temporary casing; impact-driven casing may be impossible to extract
No jetting during extraction: jet water harms the fluid concrete
Vibrations usually extremely small at 50 to 70 ft, farther in hard or cemented layers; monitor near sensitive structures (Dowding, 2000)
Most effective in sands with shallow groundwater (thin liquefied zone at the wall); hard layers may stop it
Dense soils: alternate driving and drilling, or relief drilling with an auger
Extract while the concrete is fluid: drive down a few inches to break free, then pull
figures: Figure 5-11: Extraction of Temporary Casing Using a Vibratory Hammer
sections.applicability: Vibratory installation and extraction of temporary casing; construction vibration near structures

sections.title: Twisting/Rotating Method
sections.body: [pp. 5-12 to 5-14] Casing can be advanced ahead of the excavation by a drill using special casing and tools, with a cutting shoe designed to minimize soil friction. Because of the torque needed, conventional drill rigs are limited to relatively small casing, generally less than 4 ft diameter; hydraulic fixed mast rigs with a rotary that moves on the leads are well suited (Figure 5-12, 39 inch diameter tangent piles for a retaining wall). Larger casings typically need a specialized oscillator or rotator (Chapter 4), which clamps the casing with hydraulic jaws and twists and pushes it with hydraulic pistons, reacting against a large drilling machine or temporary frame (Figure 5-13, an oscillator on a drill rig casing to top of rock before drilling the socket); soil may also be removed with a grab (Figure 5-5). The casing carries cutting teeth extending slightly beyond its outside, and the bottom section has a cutting shoe (Figure 5-14) that cuts a slightly oversized hole to relieve stress on the casing sides; the soil inside is excavated as the casing is installed. A plug of soil must remain inside the casing during installation so the bottom does not become unstable, its thickness depending on the strength and stability of the material at the casing base; in water-bearing soils the water head inside must be maintained to prevent bottom heave. Polymer or mineral fluids can be used inside but are usually avoided by keeping a soil plug and, where needed, a water head; heave into the casing would loosen the ground with adverse effects on side resistance and possible subsidence. At completion the plug may be removed to the casing base (or below) if the casing is in rock or a stable formation or a drilling fluid head is used; if the hole ends in water-bearing soil with only a water head, the casing may need to extend below the final base, which may leave an annular zone of loosened soil at the base. The thicker casing (typically about 2 to 2.5 inches) affects the cover and cage spacers; with single wall pipe and welded joints (Figure 5-6) the joints protrude inside, so the cage must be built and placed so nothing hangs on them during cage installation or casing extraction. To avoid torsional deformation of the reinforcement, the casing is typically oscillated back and forth during extraction, even if rotated continuously during installation; it is typically extracted as concrete is placed, keeping concrete head above the casing tip for positive pressure against the hole, and with exterior groundwater the head of concrete and water inside must exceed the exterior water pressure. The concrete must remain fluid so the oscillation does not twist and distort the cage.
key_points: Conventional rigs limited to casing generally less than 4 ft diameter; larger needs an oscillator or rotator
Cutting teeth and a cutting shoe cut a slightly oversized hole to relieve side stress
Keep a soil plug and water head inside to prevent bottom heave and loosening
Casing extended below the base in water-bearing soil may leave loosened soil at the base
Casing typically about 2 to 2.5 inches thick: allow for cover and spacers; protruding joints can snag the cage
Oscillate during extraction, keep concrete head above the tip and above exterior water pressure, concrete fluid

sections.title: Possible Effects of Temporary Casing on Axial and Lateral Resistance
sections.body: [pp. 5-15 to 5-17] Where temporary casing is to be used, the designer should consider its possible effects on axial and lateral resistance. In general no deleterious effect on lateral resistance should occur from removing temporary casing, except perhaps where casing in an oversized, pre-drilled hole has the soil collapse into the void outside before concrete placement and extraction, leaving loosened soil. Casing that cannot be removed and is left in an oversized hole may reduce lateral stiffness due to the void, which should be filled with grout or flowable cementitious material even if the cased zone is not relied on axially. Axial resistance can be significantly affected by the installation method. If axial resistance comes entirely from below the casing there is little concern; if the cased zone's contribution is small compared with the shaft below, it is appropriate and cost-effective to ignore it so the constructor can use the most cost-effective strategy. Where it is significant: casing in a predrilled hole may reduce side resistance if contaminants, debris or loosened soil are trapped between concrete and ground, e.g., thick heavy slurry left in the annulus, casing extracted too quickly before the slurry is displaced by concrete, or debris falling into the annulus. Where casing is placed into rock through a predrilled hole, debris is likely to collect and a good concrete to rock bond will not develop: Osterberg and Hayes (1999, Figure 5-15) report a shaft cased the full length of a 10-ft rock socket for a dry, inspectable base whose bi-directional load test measured only 50 tons of side resistance in the socket, against 1200 tons in another shaft whose casing stopped above rock with the socket built in the wet. Casing installed ahead of the excavation by vibratory hammer should generally not harm side resistance in sands and may densify them, but in cohesive soil it is likely to leave a relatively smooth surface; Camp et al. (2002) found lower side resistance in the upper marl with temporary casing than in an uncased slurry shaft, attributed to the smoother surface. Segmental casing advanced by oscillator/rotator is generally considered to have no significant effect on side resistance so long as a stable excavation is maintained; the cutting teeth and oscillation during withdrawal tend to leave a rough surface (Brown, 2012; Figure 5-16), and comparative tests (Brown, 2002; Katzenbach et al., 2008) suggest reasonably good unit side shear compared with slurry methods, possibly better than with bentonite slurry; since very large or deep bentonite shafts are hard to complete before bentonite contaminates the interface, full length segmental casing can be more favorable for achieving the design side resistance, but failure to keep the base stable loosens the soil and reduces side resistance. Where segmental casing extends below the final base (5.2.2.2.2), an annular zone of loosened soil may slightly reduce base resistance unless corrected by base grouting. If the constructor cannot extract the casing, the engineer must judge its effect on axial resistance; expedient load testing (Chapter 13) may help, and many studies show that load transfer from casing to soil can be significantly less than from concrete in contact with the soil (Li et al., 2017; Lo and Li, 2003; Owens and Reese, 1982).
key_points: Removing temporary casing generally does not harm lateral resistance; grout the void around casing left in an oversized hole
Ignore the cased zone axially when its share is small, letting the contractor choose the method
Predrilled-hole casing can trap slurry, debris or loosened soil; in rock a good bond will not develop
Osterberg and Hayes (1999): 50 tons side resistance with casing through a 10-ft socket vs 1200 tons with the socket drilled wet
Vibrated casing: fine or beneficial in sand, smoother (lower) side resistance in cohesive soil (Camp et al., 2002)
Oscillated segmental casing: rough surface, good side shear if the base stays stable
Casing left in place may transfer load significantly less than concrete against soil

sections.title: Removing Casing after Concrete Sets
sections.body: [pp. 5-17 to 5-19] Drilled shafts through a body of water typically use a permanent casing that serves as a form until the concrete sets and is then left in place, which is preferable to removal for several reasons: it adds corrosion protection for the reinforcement (chlorides must penetrate the casing as well as the cover); it avoids removal difficulties that could damage the concrete; and the concrete surface after removal can have bleed channels or other imperfections needing preparation. Perceived aesthetic benefits of exposed concrete can often be met with coatings on the casing. Figure 5-17 shows a removable casing on the I-95 Fuller Warren Bridge over the St. Johns River, Jacksonville, Florida: split the full length and joined by a mechanical pin arrangement, with a rubber gasket, the 72-inch casings were vibrated through soft river deposits to a stiff silty clay or limestone, and after the concrete set the pin mechanism was lifted to expand the joint and lift the casing off for re-use. Problems typical of such solutions arose: (a) after first use the joint was typically not water tight despite cleaning and repair; (b) the split joint was hard to open, possibly fouled with concrete; (c) once opened the casing was hard to lift off even with a vibratory hammer; (d) diver inspection found surface defects, including washout of cement next to the split joint, numerous spalls and bleed water cavities, and locally exposed reinforcement; and (e) costly underwater remediation was needed. Removable casing may thus pose a risk of structural defects, and inspection and repair under water (limited visibility, swift currents) is difficult, so removable casing at offshore foundations should generally be avoided. Where removal of exposed permanent casing is specified, it should generally be limited to the part above water, typically torch cut into sections without damaging the concrete, with exposed defects then repaired; repairs above water are easier and more reliable. An alternative with less risk (Figure 5-18) uses a temporary casing large enough to act as a cofferdam: the shaft inside (with permanent casing or in an uncased hole under drilling fluid) is concreted to below the water surface, and a removable form inside forms the column and the splice of column to shaft reinforcement; the form avoids temporary casing handling stresses, the column concrete is placed in the dry after removing laitance at the cold joint, and after the form is removed the temporary casing above the shaft cutoff is torch cut, by divers below water level.
key_points: Permanent casing through water is preferably left in place: corrosion protection, no removal damage, no surface defects
Removable split casing (I-95 Fuller Warren Bridge, 72-inch): leaking joints, stuck casing, washout, spalls, exposed steel, costly underwater repair
Avoid removable casing at offshore foundations
Remove exposed permanent casing only above water, by torch cutting, then repair
Alternative: a cofferdam-size temporary casing with a removable column form and a cold joint below water
figures: Figure 5-17: Locking Mechanism for a Removable Casing
Figure 5-18: Construction Joint Below the Water Surface
sections.applicability: Deciding whether to remove casing at over-water drilled shafts; column forming below water

sections.title: Permanent Casing
sections.body: [p. 5-20] Permanent casing remains and becomes a permanent part of the foundation. One example is a shaft installed through water with the protruding casing used as a form: a technique used successfully sets a template for positioning, sets a permanent casing through it with its top above water and its base an appropriate depth below the mudline, excavates with drilling slurry, and places concrete by tremie to the casing top. Permanent casing may be specified for a deep, large-diameter, high-capacity shaft in sound rock where control of the concrete supply may let several hours pass between the first concrete and extracting temporary casing, so the concrete may be taking its initial set when the seal is broken, making extraction difficult without damage. It is common where the shaft passes through a cavity, as in karst, as a form keeping concrete out of the cavity: besides the cost of lost concrete, flow into large cavities can mix soil or water into the shaft, producing a void, and can distort the cage. It is also common through very soft soils, such as marsh deposits, to prevent the fluid concrete bulging outward; a bulge at an extremely soft stratum risks a neck in the shaft above it or deformation of the cage. Subsections: 5.3.1 Types and Dimensions; 5.3.2 Installation; 5.3.3 Effects on Axial and Lateral Resistance.
key_points: Over water: template, permanent casing to an appropriate depth below mudline, slurry excavation, tremie concrete to the casing top
Deep high-capacity shafts in rock where temporary casing could not be pulled before the concrete sets
Through karst cavities: keeps concrete in, avoids voids, soil or water mixing and cage distortion
Through very soft soils (marsh): prevents bulging, necking and cage deformation
sections.applicability: Marine construction; soft soil environments; structural design of cased zones

sections.title: Types and Dimensions
sections.body: [pp. 5-20 to 5-21] Permanent steel casing types and dimensions are similar to temporary casing, but it can be installed in longer sections and may be driven like a steel pipe pile since it need not be extracted. Where it is a structural component, its dimensions, material properties and welds are typically shown in the contract documents and subject to quality control and documentation as for a steel pipe pile or any steel structure. Figure 5-19 (left) shows permanent casings extending into a cofferdam after the seal was placed and the cofferdam dewatered, carrying the shafts through river water to rock; the bond between casing and seal concrete was designed to engage the shafts' axial resistance against uplift water pressure on the seal, reducing its thickness compared with a seal relying on concrete dead weight alone; the right photo shows the reinforcement after the exposed casings were removed. Corrugated metal pipe (CMP, Figure 5-20) is sometimes used as a shallow liner because of its low cost, but it is relatively flexible and cannot take installation stresses like thicker steel pipe. A semi-rigid liner, or a low-friction coating such as bitumen, may be used to minimize skin friction from downdrag or expansive soils; liners of two concentric pressed-fiber tubes separated by a thin asphalt coating have reduced skin friction in expansive soils by as much as 90 per cent compared with no liner. Flexible liners (plastic sheets, rubber-coated membranes or mesh) are used infrequently in the United States: the cage is encased in the liner before placement in a dry or dewatered hole and concrete is tremied inside, to keep concrete out of a side cavity or caving soil off the cage. They apply only where the shaft develops its required resistance entirely below the liner, since skin friction in the liner zone cannot be computed with any accuracy.
key_points: Similar to temporary casing; longer sections, may be driven like a pipe pile
Structural casing: dimensions, properties and welds in the contract documents, with QC as for steel piles
Casing-to-seal bond can engage shaft uplift resistance and thin the cofferdam seal
CMP liners are cheap but flexible
Semi-rigid liners or bitumen coatings cut downdrag or expansive-soil friction; double pressed-fiber tubes with asphalt cut it by as much as 90 per cent
Flexible liners only where all resistance is developed below the liner

Figure 5-20: Corrugated Metal Pipe (CMP) Used as Permanent Liner
sections.applicability: Specifying permanent casing and liners, including liners against downdrag or expansive soils

sections.title: Installation of Permanent Casing
sections.body: [p. 5-22] Permanent steel casing may be installed by any of the methods for temporary casing, or driven with an impact hammer. Casing placed in an oversized hole may be sealed into rock by twisting or driving, and the annulus often must be filled with tremie grout to transfer lateral soil resistance, unless the overburden is neglected for lateral loading or subject to scour. Driving can be effective and efficient since the casing need not be extracted, but driving stresses require a drivability evaluation as in the FHWA Driven Pile Manual (FHWA-NHI-16-009, Hannigan et al., 2016). Driving large pipe into hard soils or rock is limited, and boulders are particularly troublesome; impact driving into rock or boulders can deform the casing end so drill tools cannot pass, in which case placing the casing in a pre-drilled hole may be more attractive.
key_points: Any temporary casing method, or impact driving
Grout the annulus of casing in an oversized hole for lateral resistance, unless the overburden is neglected or scourable
Check drivability (FHWA-NHI-16-009, Hannigan et al., 2016); rock and boulders can deform the casing toe
sections.applicability: Installing permanent casing by driving or in oversized holes; drivability and annulus grouting

sections.title: Effects of Permanent Casing on Axial and Lateral Resistance
sections.body: [pp. 5-22 to 5-23] If the soil in the cased zone is scourable or cannot contribute significantly, its resistance should not be counted and the installation method is unimportant from this view. If it is to contribute significantly to axial resistance, the casing must be installed to give good load transfer in side resistance; casing in an oversized hole generally cannot be relied upon for axial load transfer. Even with no axial reliance, where lateral resistance is needed in the zone of casing in an oversized hole the annulus should be grouted. An unfilled annulus can also be an unintended seepage conduit, a problem near flood control levees or other water retention structures or where aquifers could be cross-contaminated in contaminated areas, and expansive soil or rock at depth may see increased water content from water migrating down the casing. Casing driven with an impact hammer and left in place should provide axial side resistance similar to a driven steel pipe pile and may be treated as such (Caltrans: Cast-in-Steel-Shell, CISS, pile); vibrated casing may give less side resistance than impact-driven casing, and the usual methods for steel piles may not apply. Permanent casing can add to the structural capacity and bending stiffness of the shaft (Chapter 12), but corrosion reduces its thickness with time and should be considered. Aggressive conditions are a particular concern for casing in fill, low pH soils and marine environments, identified from properties of the fill, natural soil and groundwater: aggressive if soil pH is less than 4.5 or resistivity is less than 2000 ohm-cm; chloride and/or sulfate content should be tested for resistivity between 2000 and 5000 ohm-cm, conditions being aggressive if sulfate exceeds 200 ppm or chloride exceeds 100 ppm; soils with resistivity greater than 5000 ohm-cm are non-aggressive. Hannigan et al. (2016) give a conservative corrosion rate of 0.003 inch/year for steel piles in fill or disturbed natural soil; see FHWA-NHI-16-009, AASHTO R 27-01 (2004) and FHWA-NHI-00-043 (Elias et al., 2001).
key_points: Do not count soil in a scourable or minor cased zone
Casing in an oversized hole generally cannot be relied on for axial load transfer; grout the annulus if lateral resistance is needed
An open annulus is a seepage path (levees, aquifer cross-contamination, wetting expansive strata)
Impact-driven casing acts like a driven steel pipe pile (CISS); vibrated casing may give less side resistance
Casing adds structural capacity and stiffness (Chapter 12), reduced by corrosion
Aggressive: pH < 4.5, resistivity < 2000 ohm-cm, sulfate > 200 ppm or chloride > 100 ppm (test at 2000-5000 ohm-cm); > 5000 ohm-cm non-aggressive
Conservative corrosion rate 0.003 inch/year in fill or disturbed soil (Hannigan et al., 2016)
sections.applicability: Counting permanent casing in axial, lateral and structural design; corrosion allowance

sections.title: Construction Using Drilling Fluids
sections.body: [p. 5-23] Drilling fluids within the hole are another means of stabilizing a drilled shaft excavation: water, or water mixed with minerals (typically bentonite clay) or synthetic polymers. They provide stability by a fluid pressure inside the excavation greater than the groundwater pressure, preventing destabilizing seepage into the hole (Figure 5-21). Additives (bentonite or polymer) help contain the fluid in the hole and minimize fluid loss through the borehole wall, so the positive head can be maintained; water with additives is typically called slurry, and the technique slurry drilling. Subsections: 5.4.1 Water; 5.4.2 Mineral; 5.4.3 Synthetic; 5.4.4 Mineral/Polymer Blended; 5.4.5 Quality Control and Inspection; 5.4.6 Effects on Axial Resistance.
key_points: Fluid pressure above groundwater pressure prevents destabilizing inflow
Bentonite or polymer additives limit fluid loss so the positive head is kept (slurry drilling)
figures: Figure 5-21: Differential Fluid Head Pressure Used to Maintain Borehole Stability
sections.applicability: Below-water-table construction; cohesionless soils; unstable conditions

sections.title: Water as a Drilling Fluid
sections.body: [pp. 5-23 to 5-25] Water alone is not typically suitable in uncemented granular soils, because it flows out too fast to keep a positive head and gives no stabilizing effect; it can be used effectively where the soil is sufficiently cemented or the uncased excavation is entirely in rock. In a wet but otherwise stable excavation through pervious rock or other strong material, the hole may simply be filled with water to counter seepage into it, e.g., where casing seated in rock is not watertight; inflow may wash fines in and create voids around the casing base, causing subsidence or loss of support (Figure 5-22). Seepage during concrete placement (Figure 5-23) harms concrete quality, since groundwater keeps entering the mix until enough concrete head is established; water should be added to counterbalance it, and a positive head before concrete placement protects the mix. As a general guide, seepage exceeding more than one inch in 5 minutes is excessive and the hole should be flooded before concrete placement. A positive water head may be needed where full length casing supports permeable or unstable soils (Figure 5-24), to avoid upward flow into the base that could soften the base material or pipe cohesionless soil, possibly with soil flowing up into the casing, loosening and surface subsidence; a positive head, often with a soil plug at the casing bottom, mitigates this (5.2.2.2). Water is also the flushing fluid for rock tools such as percussion tools, double walled core barrels and full face rotary tools; air may flush some tools with the hole kept full of water for positive head (Chapter 4).
key_points: Water alone is unsuitable in uncemented granular soils; usable in cemented soil or rock
Fill a seeping but stable hole with water to stop inflow washing fines and undermining the casing
Seepage of more than one inch in 5 minutes is excessive: flood the hole before concrete placement
Fully cased holes in permeable soil need a positive water head (often with a soil plug) against base heave or piping
Water or air flushing for percussion, double-wall core barrel and full face rock tools

sections.title: Mineral Drilling Fluid
sections.body: [pp. 5-25 to 5-30] Bentonite clay is the most commonly used mineral additive, widely used in oilfield drilling; composed mainly of montmorillonite, it absorbs many times its weight of water, and small amounts form a colloidal bentonite slurry that increases viscosity over water with a small increase in unit weight, looking like chocolate milk (Figure 5-25). Much North American construction bentonite comes from Wyoming (named for the Benton Shale); the desirable grade is high grade sodium bentonite, which hydrates more water per unit weight than other clays (e.g., calcium bentonite), so the fluid holds relatively little suspended solid when introduced. Some of the minerals are filtered out at the borehole wall as fluid passes into the soil, forming a filter cake that reduces permeability and helps contain the fluid (Figure 5-26); this is the main difference from other construction fluids, greatly improving stability but able to harm the concrete-soil bond. A positive head above the surrounding groundwater must be kept; the stabilizing pressure at a depth comes from the head differential and unit weight (Figure 5-27). Bentonite slurry typically weighs 65 to 70 pcf, against 62.4 pcf for fresh water. A 10-ft head differential is generally desirable, but with bentonite a 5-ft minimum is often sufficient because of the unit weight difference; the filter cake also concentrates the pressure gradient at the face. Bentonite must be mixed with vigorous shearing and hydrated (typically 24 hrs minimum) before use (mixing plant, Figure 5-28), which also minimizes unmixed clay that could contaminate concrete or build thick filter cake. Because of excess filter cake, exposure time before concreting should be limited: rarely an issue for small shafts completed in a day, but a consideration for large or deep holes left overnight; if excavation and concreting cannot start within a few hours, filter cake may need active removal with a bucket with a sidewall wire brush or an auger with protruding perimeter teeth (Chapter 4), followed promptly by final cleanout, rebar and concrete. Bentonite can also harm axial resistance where rock socket side resistance is important. In large-pore formations (gravelly soils, poorly graded coarse sands) filter cake may not form well; bentonite may still work in gravel with enough fines and gel strength, otherwise casing, additives, other fluids or grouting may be needed. Unit weight and suspended solids must be controlled: after mixing, mineral slurry has a specific gravity typically about 1.03 to 1.05, and unit weight and viscosity rise as excavated particles are picked up. Below a certain concentration particles stay suspended long enough to pump the slurry out or be displaced by high-slump concrete, but the slurry must be cleaned before concreting, since excess solids settle on the inspected base or onto the concrete, entrapping sand pockets; a small amount remains suspended for a short (hour or less) placement, but large deep shafts placed over several hours need cleaner slurry. Sand is removed with a de-sanding unit (Figure 5-29) of cyclones and screens removing sand-sized and larger particles, fluid pumped from the base by airlift or hydraulic pump while fresh slurry is added at the top, then checked for sand content, density and viscosity; silt and clay can be removed by centrifuge, but slurry too heavy or viscous despite low sand content is normally discarded and replaced. High-salt groundwater may flocculate bentonite; it can be used for limited periods in saline water by premixing with fresh water and adding e.g. potassium acetate to impede salt entering the diffuse double layer, but salt eventually flocculates it, so watch continuously and be ready to exchange slurry. Attapulgite and sepiolite are used in limited amounts, typically for permeable soils in saline settings near their sources (e.g., Georgia, Florida, Nevada); they do not hydrate, so do not flocculate in salt water, need very vigorous and continual remixing, can be used as soon as mixed, and form soft thick clay zones on the wall rather than a solid filter cake, generally controlling filtration and easily scoured by rising concrete. Compatibility of the mineral with groundwater chemistry should be verified, especially with low pH or contamination. Disposal of bentonite (turbidity, hard to remove once mixed) can be a significant cost or environmental consideration.
key_points: High grade sodium bentonite forms a filter cake: better stability, but can harm concrete-soil bond
Bentonite slurry typically 65 to 70 pcf vs 62.4 pcf for water; specific gravity about 1.03 to 1.05 after mixing
10-ft head differential desirable; 5-ft minimum often sufficient with bentonite
Hydrate typically 24 hrs minimum with vigorous shear mixing
Limit open time; remove filter cake (wire brush bucket, toothed auger) if concreting cannot start within a few hours
Clean slurry before concreting with de-sanders; discard heavy or viscous slurry
Salt water flocculates bentonite; attapulgite or sepiolite for saline sites
Bentonite disposal can be costly

sections.title: Synthetic Drilling Fluid
sections.body: [pp. 5-30 to 5-33] In the last 20 years synthetic (polymer) drilling fluids have replaced bentonite slurry on most drilled shaft applications in North America, although prevalence varies locally, and their use worldwide has increased dramatically. The polymers are long chain-like hydrocarbon molecules interacting with each other, the soil and the water to increase viscosity; the fluid looks slippery, slimy and viscous (Figure 5-30). The strands form a three-dimensional web (scanning electron micro-photograph at 800 times, Figure 5-31(a)) that can form a membrane on the sidewall (Figure 5-31(b)) if a positive head is kept, sometimes seen as a sticky wetted surface on excavated soil clumps with little fluid penetration. There is no filter cake as with bentonite, so polymers may lose more fluid to the soil with time, but the widely used polymers have not shown the detrimental effect on concrete/soil bond associated with bentonite filter cake. Polymers come in liquid or dry granular form and are mixed and hydrated before use (Figure 5-32), needing much less material than bentonite for a similar volume; mixing disperses the polymer, but shearing by some pumps (good for bentonite) breaks the long chains and is avoided, and for the same reason polymers are not typically used with circulation drilling or hydromills for diaphragm walls or barrettes (4.2.3.6, 4.2.4). Polymer adds little weight, so with low unit weight, no filter cake and possible fluid loss, the positive fluid head is critically important. Polymer fluids tend not to incorporate dispersive clays, which also helps preserve rock sockets in clay-shales prone to rapid weathering (Axtell et al., 2009). Polymers do not hold soils in suspension, so even silt can settle after excavation if the slurry is not cleaned; de-sanding plants are unsuitable (screens clog, shearing breaks the polymer). Polymer is typically cleaned by adding flocculating agents and allowing quiet time for settling; good practice is a full exchange with fresh slurry, pumping from the base to holding tanks (Figure 5-33). Afterwards a de-activating agent (bleach works on most polymers) breaks the polymer down so solids drop out, making disposal relatively cheap and easy. The printed comparison table (p. 5-33, unnumbered), polymer vs. bentonite: easy to mix, less time to hydrate vs. mixing and hydration more involved; time required for de-sanding and removal of fines vs. de-sanding equipment and handling more efficient; no filter cake, so greater fluid loss and less stabilization of the hole vs. filter cake plus weight improves stabilization, especially in coarse granular soils; no filter cake, so less detrimental impact on side resistance vs. filter cake can affect side resistance (exposure time should be limited; additional preparation may be needed); polymers can break down due to shearing and pumping but are easy to dispose vs. generally more costly to dispose but easier to reuse.
key_points: Polymer fluids have replaced bentonite on most North American drilled shafts in the last 20 years
No filter cake: more fluid loss, but no bentonite-type loss of concrete/soil bond
Avoid shearing pumps; not typical with circulation drilling or hydromills
Low unit weight and no filter cake: the positive head is critical
Does not hold soil in suspension: clean by flocculation and settling or full exchange; de-sanders unsuitable
Helps preserve clay-shale sockets (Axtell et al., 2009); easy disposal after bleach de-activation
Comparison table p. 5-33: polymer easier to mix and dispose; bentonite stabilizes better, de-sands more efficiently, reuses more easily

sections.title: Mineral/Polymer Blended Drilling Fluid
sections.body: [pp. 5-33 to 5-34] Blended slurries of minerals (generally bentonite) and polymers can in some situations be designed to take advantage of each, e.g., polymer in bentonite can minimize filter cake thickness and reduce the tendency to incorporate native clays (and increase density, viscosity, etc.). Blended fluids are a specialty field needing expertise beyond what is normally available on most drilled shaft projects, with relatively little U.S. experience; specifications for mineral or commercial polymer slurries likely will not suit blends, and blending is not recommended unless those involved can set appropriate specifications and QC/QA procedures for the site conditions. Packaged blends are marketed as extended bentonites: the polymer reduces the bentonite needed, an economic consideration as high-quality bentonite becomes harder to find, but properties depend significantly on the polymer, so the contractor should work closely with the supplier.
key_points: Blends can thin filter cake and limit clay pickup
Specialty field with little U.S. experience; standard slurry specifications likely unsuitable
Not recommended without the expertise to set specifications and QC/QA
Extended bentonites: work closely with the supplier
sections.applicability: Considering blended or extended bentonite slurries

sections.title: Quality Control and Inspection
sections.body: [pp. 5-34 to 5-39] Cleaning the excavation: both the base and the fluid should be reasonably clean and free of debris. Excess cuttings on the base can affect base resistance through compressible material and, even where base resistance matters little, can mix into the concrete during tremie placement and cause defects; excess suspended solids settling during placement also contaminate concrete. Perfect cleaning is neither possible nor necessary, a small amount on the base typically having little or no consequence. A typical specification (Chapter 14) allows no more than three inches of sediment or loose or disturbed material just before concrete placement, and 50 percent or more of the base area with no more than 1/2 inch where base resistance in rock or strong material is used in design; some agencies limit the maximum to 1-1/2 inches for shafts relying on base resistance for a large part of the axial resistance. A flat-bottomed cleanout bucket (Figure 5-34) may remove debris, especially after a quiet period; with an unagitated fluid most solids may settle overnight and a few passes remove them (Chapter 4). If many passes are needed they may stir up sediment, and a pump is more effective: airlift or hydraulic pumps (Figures 5-35, 5-36) lift sediment-laden fluid from the base while clean fluid is added at the top. Airlifts inject air into the bottom of the fluid-filled pipe and buoyancy drives circulation; a hydraulic pump is easier to control, whereas an airlift can pump so fast that keeping the hole recharged and the essential positive head is a challenge. After cleaning, the base is inspected against the project requirements (Guide Specifications, Appendix D; inspection methods, Chapter 15). Figure 5-37 shows the cut, inverted base of an exhumed 6-ft shaft built under slurry, bearing the cleanout bucket's impression: evidence that a slurry shaft base can be cleaned effectively with the correct equipment and techniques. Sampling and testing the drilling fluid checks it against accepted guidelines and the project specifications, most importantly just before concrete placement but also for stability during excavation; samples are taken through the column (sampler, Figure 5-38(a)), those near the bottom being important as they hold the most sediment. Viscosity is measured indirectly with the Marsh funnel (Figure 5-38(b)), timing a volume of slurry: water takes about 26 seconds per quart and bentonite fluid typically 30 to 45 seconds; many specifications allow 28 to 50 seconds depending on the application. Higher viscosity aids stability, but bentonite filter cake could become thick enough to harm side resistance; polymers are often used at higher viscosity, 32 to 135 seconds, because without filter cake more viscosity may be needed to limit fluid loss and there is no filter cake concern. The mud balance (Figure 5-39(a)) measures unit weight: bentonite fluid with excessive density is likely too contaminated with soil for concrete placement, though heavy slurry aids stability; density is not normally an issue for polymer. Sand content (Figure 5-39(b)) measures suspended particles not passing a #200 sieve; upper limits before concrete placement of 4% for bentonite and 1% for polymer are typical and routinely specified, and may need to be well below these for large or deep shafts: concreting a 3-ft diameter, 40 ft deep shaft may take only 15 to 20 minutes, but an 8-ft, 150 ft deep shaft may take several hours; more restrictive sand content limits are recommended for any case where concrete placement under slurry can extend beyond two hours. Hardness, as indicated by pH, matters for bentonite or polymer and is normally checked at the start with the make-up water; it is particularly important for polymers, and soda ash is typically used to raise pH. A filter-press (not a routine inspection test) indicates the tendency to form filter cake, useful for controlling bentonite cake thickness: slurry is forced through filter paper at 100 psi for 30 minutes, the free water recovered is measured in cubic centimeters and the cake thickness to the nearest millimeter after washing off superficial slurry.
key_points: Typical spec (Chapter 14): no more than 3 inches of sediment before concreting; 50 percent or more of the base with no more than 1/2 inch where base resistance in rock or strong material is used
Some agencies limit base sediment to 1-1/2 inches where base resistance carries much of the load
Cleanout bucket after a quiet period, then airlift or hydraulic pump; keep the positive head while pumping
Sample through the column, especially near the bottom
Marsh funnel: water about 26 s/quart; bentonite typically 30 to 45 s, specs often 28 to 50 s; polymer 32 to 135 s
Mud balance for unit weight: heavy bentonite slurry is too contaminated for concreting
Sand content before concreting: 4% bentonite, 1% polymer; tighter where placement may exceed two hours
pH checked on make-up water (soda ash raises it); filter-press at 100 psi for 30 minutes for bentonite cake

sections.title: Effects of Drilling Fluid on Axial Resistance
sections.body: [pp. 5-39 to 5-41] The most important influence of drilling fluid on axial resistance is a positive one: keeping a stable hole and the integrity of the bearing materials. The caving in Figure 5-40 might have been avoided with drilling fluid or casing; seepage into the hole, even with casing, can carry debris to the bottom and harms concrete quality. With the practices above it is often easier to clean the bottom under fluid than in a dry hole. Proper fluid with good base cleaning avoids the soft toe effect of Figure 5-41(a), where a small duck tail at the start of the load test shows little initial base resistance, stiffening after about 1/2 inch of displacement, the debris requiring larger displacement to mobilize base resistance; Figure 5-41(b), two load tests on rock near Atlanta with a clean base (test shaft 1 on weathered rock, test shaft 2 on hard rock), shows high base resistance at very small displacements. Excess bentonite filter cake could harm side resistance, and there is increasing evidence that unit side resistance in granular soil is superior with polymer fluids than with bentonite, even with accepted practices (Figure 5-42, an early full scale comparison, Brown, 2002, corroborated by other studies); the effect is not expected or observed in low-permeability cohesive soils, likely because no fluid loss means no filter cake. Side resistance in either case is mobilized at small displacements but is ductile out to nearly 2 inches, not dropping away in a brittle manner, though its magnitude clearly depends on construction means and methods. Polymers also tend to reduce wetting and degradation of shales at the borehole wall, which could otherwise leave socket side resistance governed by degraded rather than intact shale; slake durability tests (Axtell et al., 2009) and anecdotal load test evidence support the benefit of polymers in preserving shale bearing materials.
key_points: Main effect is positive: a stable hole and intact bearing material
Base cleaning under fluid avoids the soft toe effect (stiffening after about 1/2 inch)
Polymer gives higher unit side resistance than bentonite in granular soils (Brown, 2002); not in low-permeability cohesive soils
Side resistance mobilized at small displacement and ductile to nearly 2 inches
Polymers reduce shale degradation in sockets (Axtell et al., 2009)

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described techniques for maintaining stable drilled shaft excavations: naturally stable conditions (dry, cohesive, intact rock); temporary casing (tool casing); permanent casing; and drilling fluids (water, bentonite, polymer, blended). Excavation stability must be maintained from start of drilling through completion of concrete placement and casing extraction. Contractor chooses appropriate method; designer must understand implications of each method for shaft performance and design.
